title: The Contamination Clock: Evaluation Validity as Runtime Statein Adaptive AI Systems
content: Adaptive AI systems change after evaluation through updates to models, memory, prompts, and tools. Yet, an earlierscore may remain numerically correct while no longer describing the current system. Reuse of evaluation outcomesfor optimization can also compromise the independence of that evidence. Here, we introduce the ContaminationClock, a runtime protocol that links scores to system snapshots and evaluation histories. We isolate measurement fromupdates and record provenance and reuse to assess historical validity, current applicability, and permission for reuseseparately. In three prospective studies, we tested whether memory containing evaluation outcomes preferentiallyimproved performance on reused tasks. In the first study, we found greater gains on reused than on sealed tasks in allten evaluation episodes after adjustment for matched unrelated memory (mean adjusted contrast 0.469; 95% interval[0.377, 0.560]). We reproduced this advantage in another model class, while unrelated-memory shams yielded anear-zero mean contrast. By varying exposure, we further showed that the mean contrast rose from 0.119 to 0.453 asexact traces were supplied for 25% to 100% of reused tasks. We also found that token reordering preserved the meancontrast, whereas removing the verified decision from each trace reduced it to−0.013. By comparison, a leak-freefine-tuning update did not trigger the contamination alert (differential point estimate 0.069; frozen bounds ±0.12). Inthis controlled test, we nevertheless treated the earlier claim as superseded because the model had changed. This workprovides a protocol for making reevaluation an explicit, auditable part of agent development while preserving validhistorical evidence. Future studies with larger models and semantic memory could test whether the protocol keepsperformance claims reliable across successive updates.
